Mihai wants to go to Atocha station. He stops a lady in the street.
Excuse me, madam. Where is Atocha station?
Atocha? It’s quite far. Are you walking?
Well, straight ahead along this street. Then, turn right.
Yes. There’s a big square there. The station is next to the museum.
Yes, in the square, to the left of the bank.
And how long does it take on foot?
About twenty minutes. Otherwise, the metro is here, fifty metres away.

a + el = to the / next to (with “lado”)
CH is read like the English “ch” in “church”: Atocha = “a-to-cha”, mucho = “moo-cho”.
R at the end of a word is short, a single tap: ir, comer, lugar. Don’t roll it.
1. The verb IR (to go): completely irregular
IR doesn’t look like anything else, so it’s learned by heart. The good news: the forms are short.
The forms of IR look like the endings of -ar verbs: v + oy, as, a, amos, ais, an. And “¡Vamos!” = “Let’s go! / Come on!” is heard everywhere in Spain.
2. IR A + place; AL = a + el
After IR comes “a” (to): “Voy a Madrid” = “I’m going to Madrid”.
When “a” meets the article “el”, they MUST merge into “al”.
“Voy a el museo” is wrong. Always “al museo”. The merging only happens with “el”, not with “la”, “los”, “las”.
A trick for left/right: deREcha has the “r” of “Right”. Izquierda = left.
4. How to ask for help politely
In the street, with strangers, use “usted”. These phrases work anywhere:
Excuse me, where is the metro?
Excuse me, is there a bank nearby?
How do I get to the station?
If you don’t understand the answer, ask: “Más despacio, por favor” (more slowly, please) or “¿Puede repetir?” (could you repeat that?).
5. How you travel: EN metro, A pie
English says “by metro”. Spanish uses “en”, without an article:
A typical mistake: “Voy con el metro” or “Voy por metro”. The correct form is “Voy en metro”.

Tom is on a trip to Toledo with his Spanish class.
Toledo is an old city with lots of small, narrow streets.
At twelve, the teacher says: “You have two hours free. At two, everyone in Plaza de Zocodover.”
Tom goes to the cathedral, then visits a museum and buys a souvenir.
At half past one he looks at his watch. Where is the square? He doesn’t know. He has no map, and his phone’s battery is dead.
All the streets look the same.
Then he sees an elderly lady with a bag of bread.
“Excuse me, madam, where is Plaza de Zocodover?”.
“It’s very close,” she answers. “Straight ahead along this street, then left and left again.”
Tom goes straight ahead, turns left… and he’s in front of the cathedral again.
Luckily, the lady with the bread is there. She laughs and says: “Come on, I’ll go with you.”
At five past two, Tom arrives in the square with his new friend. The whole class applauds.
